nameStory: Sorghum gets its name from the Italian 'sorgo,' which came from Latin 'Syricum granum' meaning 'Syrian grain.' This reflects its ancient journey from Africa through the Middle East to Europe, where people knew it as grain from Syria. The species name 'bicolor' refers to the two-toned appearance of its seed heads, which often show contrasting colors.
description: Sorghum is a tall, sturdy grass that can reach 6-15 feet high, originally from Africa but now grown worldwide as an important grain crop. It looks like a robust corn plant with a thick, sturdy stem and broad leaves that arch gracefully from the main stalk. At the top, it produces dense, branched seed heads that can be white, red, brown, or yellow, packed with small, round grains. In New England, you'll mostly see it as an escaped farm crop or in wildlife food plots.

idTips.label: Seed Head
idTips.description: Dense, branched cluster at the top of the plant, 6-12 inches long, packed with small round grains that feel hard when ripe and can range from white to deep red or brown

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Broad, corn-like leaves up to 2 inches wide with a prominent white midrib running down the center, feeling smooth on top but slightly rough underneath

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Thick, sturdy stalks that feel solid and pithy when squeezed, often with a waxy coating that makes them feel slightly slippery

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in upright clumps 6-15 feet tall with multiple tillers (shoots) from the base, creating a fountain-like appearance

idTips.label: Root System
idTips.description: Develops prop roots near the base that emerge above ground to help support the tall, heavy stems

habitat: In New England, sorghum appears mainly as an escape from cultivation in disturbed soils near farms, along field edges, and in wildlife food plots. It prefers well-drained, fertile soils in full sun and doesn't tolerate frost, so it's most commonly seen in warmer, protected areas of southern New England.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring when soil temperatures warm, producing small grass-like shoots that are hard to identify at this stage.
seasonality.summer: Rapid growth occurs through summer, developing the characteristic broad leaves and thick stems, with flowering beginning in mid to late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seed heads mature and turn their final colors in early fall, becoming dry and papery before the first frost kills the plant.
seasonality.winter: Dead stalks may persist through winter as brown, dried stems, but the annual plants don't survive freezing temperatures.

funFact: Sorghum can survive droughts that would kill corn because it can go dormant during dry spells, then 'wake up' and resume growing when rain returns - making it one of the most drought-tolerant grain crops on Earth!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with corn when young, but sorghum leaves have a distinctive white midrib and the mature seed head is a branched cluster rather than corn's single cob. Johnson grass (its weedy relative) looks similar but spreads by underground runners and has looser, more open seed heads.
contextualKnowledge: Though sorghum is the world's fifth most important grain crop, many New Englanders have never heard of it since it's primarily grown in warmer, drier regions. What you see here are likely escapes from bird seed mixes or wildlife plantings rather than intentional crops.
compareHints: Sorghum differs from its notorious relative Johnson grass by being an annual that grows from seed each year rather than a perennial that spreads by underground rhizomes. Sorghum also tends to be taller and more robust with denser, more compact seed heads, while Johnson grass has more open, branched seed clusters and forms spreading colonies.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Johnson grass differs from its cultivated cousin grain sorghum by its much more aggressive spreading habit and smaller seeds.
